title: A web server with node:http

story: The broker is our only door to GitHub, Jira and Slack: when Nova, our agent that turns a Jira ticket into a pull request, wants to push a branch or post a comment, it asks the broker, and the broker does it with credentials Nova never sees. Like the gateway, our door to Claude, it is a plain Node web server with no framework at all, so that a reviewer can read every line of it.

That has a price. On its first day a test script sends the broker a 2 GB request by mistake, the broker tries to hold all of it in memory, and it crashes. Every running Nova loses its door to GitHub at the same moment. The same week someone calls a path nobody wrote, and the request simply hangs until the caller stops waiting, because no line of code ever answered it.
hook.question: When no framework does it for me, what must my own request handler do so that every request gets a clear answer and no caller can crash the service?

p: Node's built-in node:http module gives you createServer. You pass it one function, the handler, and Node calls that function for every request that arrives, whatever the path or method. The handler gets two objects: req, the incoming request with its method, URL and headers, and res, the response you write. listen(8080) opens the port. That is all a server is.

There is no router. If you want GET /health to answer ok and everything else to answer 404, you check req.method and req.url yourself. And there is no default answer either: a response is finished only when your code calls res.end(). If a request reaches a path where your handler never calls it, Node keeps the connection open and the caller waits, which is exactly the hanging request from the story.

code.file: src/hang.ts (a server with a hole in it)

notes.text: One handler for every request. req is an IncomingMessage and res a ServerResponse.
end() sends the body and finishes the response. Status 200 is the default.
Any other request reaches the end of the function without an answer, and the caller waits until it times out.

read.see:
$ curl -sS --max-time 3 localhost:8080/v1/comments
curl: (28) Operation timed out after 3005 milliseconds with 0 bytes received

read.h: A body is a stream, so count it as it arrives
p: The body of a POST request does not arrive as one string. req is a stream: the bytes come in chunks, as the client sends them, and you collect them yourself. for await over req gives you each chunk as a Buffer, the Node type for raw bytes, and Buffer.concat joins them at the end.

Nothing in Node limits how many chunks a client may send. If you simply collect everything, a 2 GB body becomes 2 GB of memory, and the process dies. So we count the bytes while they arrive and stop at a limit. The broker allows 1 MiB, 1,048,576 bytes, which is far more than any comment or run scope needs. Past that, readBody throws its own error, TooLarge, and the rest of the body is never stored.

notes.text: Only a type comes from node:http here, so it is an import type.
Our own error class, so the handler can recognise it and answer 413.
Each chunk as the client sends it. We count before we keep it.
Stop at once. The bytes after this point are never held in memory.

read.h: Every path ends with a status
p: Now the whole handler. We join the method and the path into one string, such as POST /v1/comments, and compare it with the routes we know, which is the entire router. Every path through the function ends by sending a status code, because callers and tests act on the status, not on the message. 200 means OK and 201 means created. 400 means your request is wrong, 401 means we do not know who you are, 404 means no such route, and 413 means the body is too large. 500 means the fault is ours.

The try and catch around the routes turn errors into statuses: our TooLarge becomes 413, a SyntaxError from JSON.parse becomes 400, and anything we did not expect becomes 500, so no error can leave a request hanging. The log line on a 500 names the route and never the body, because a body can hold a prompt or a token.

notes.text: One helper for every JSON answer: status, content type and body, then end().
req.url is only the path and the query. new URL needs a base to parse it; the host part is never used.
Method and path in one string. Our router is a list of if statements.
A SyntaxError here becomes 400 below. The "as" only tells TypeScript what we hope; lesson p1-5 replaces it with a real check.
Anything we did not name gets a clear 404 instead of a hang.
Log the route, never the body.

read.see:
$ curl -s -w ' [%{http_code}]\n' -X POST localhost:8080/v1/comments -d '{"text":"Plan v2 is ready"}'
{"count":1} [201]
$ curl -s -w ' [%{http_code}]\n' -X POST localhost:8080/v1/comments --data-binary @big.json
{"error":"body over 1048576 bytes"} [413]

deeper.h: Go deeper: why listen() lives in its own file
p: server.ts only builds the server, and main.ts makes it listen on the port from the PORT environment variable. Tests import server.ts and start it on a port of their own, so two test files never fight over 8080 (lesson p1-6 does this with port 0, which asks the operating system for any free port).

main.ts is also where a real service listens for SIGTERM, the signal Docker and Kubernetes send to stop a process. On SIGTERM the service calls server.close(), which stops new connections and lets open requests finish, and then exits. Lesson p1-8 shows what happens to a container that ignores the signal.

lab.title: A comments service that always answers
lab.goal: Build a small node:http service where every request gets a status, and a body over 1 MiB gets 413 instead of filling memory.

guess.q: src/hang.ts only answers GET /health. You send GET /v1/comments to it. What does curl get back?

options.text: A 404, because Node answers unknown paths for you.
options.why: Node has no idea which paths you meant to support. Only your handler can answer, and here it does not.

options.text: A 500, because the handler returned without a response.
options.why: Returning without calling end() is not an error to Node. The connection just stays open.

options.text: Nothing: the request hangs until curl stops waiting.
options.why: A response finishes only when your code calls res.end(). No end, no answer, and the caller waits.

lab.build: Add an answer for a known path with the wrong method. Today DELETE /v1/comments gets 404, which is misleading, because the path exists. Make it answer 405 Method Not Allowed with an Allow header that says GET, POST, and an empty body; every other unknown route must still get 404. Restart the server, then check it with curl -s -i -X DELETE localhost:8080/v1/comments (the -i prints the status line and the headers). Stop the server with Ctrl+C when you are done.
checks: src/hang.ts answered /health with ok [200] and let /v1/comments time out.
POST /v1/comments with a JSON body answered [201], and GET /v1/comments then listed the comment.
A body that is not JSON got [400], and the 2 MB body got [413] with body over 1048576 bytes.
curl -s -i -X DELETE localhost:8080/v1/comments starts with HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed and shows allow: GET, POST.

solution.text:
if (url.pathname === "/v1/comments") return void res.writeHead(405, { allow: "GET, POST" }).end();
    return send(res, 404, { error: "not found" });

lab.fix: A long comment from a person got 413, so someone made the limit "generous": readBody(req, Infinity). Make the same change, restart, and send big.json again: it is accepted with 201, and GET /v1/comments now sends 2 MB back. Explain what a 2 GB body would do to the broker and to every Nova run that needs it, then put the 1 MiB limit back and answer the person's problem another way.
explain: Why does a request to a path your handler does not handle hang, instead of getting an error?
Why do we count the body's bytes while the chunks arrive, instead of checking the length after reading it all?
Which status does each of these get, and why: an unknown path, bad JSON, a 2 MB body, and a bug in our code?
lab.done: Every curl in the lab gets a status (200, 201, 400, 404, 405 or 413), none of them hangs, and the server is stopped.

check.q: Your handler only has if statements for GET /health and POST /v1/comments. A caller sends GET /v1/comment (a typo). What should your code do, and why?

options.text: Nothing; Node answers 404 for paths you did not register
options.why: node:http has no list of registered paths. Without your own answer the request hangs until the caller stops waiting.

options.text: End the handler with a 404 for every route it did not match
options.why: Every path through the handler must end the response. A final 404 turns a typo into a clear answer instead of a hang.

options.text: Answer 500, because the caller hit a bug
options.why: 500 says the fault is ours. A wrong path is the caller's mistake, and 404 says exactly that.

check.q: Why does readBody count bytes inside the for await loop instead of reading the whole body and then checking body.length?

options.text: Because by the time you could check the length, a huge body would already be in memory
options.why: Counting while the chunks arrive lets you stop after 1 MiB. Checking afterwards means a 2 GB body has already filled the memory you wanted to protect.

options.text: Because body.length counts characters, not bytes
options.why: That difference is real for text with accents or emoji, but it is not the reason. The point is to stop before storing the body.

options.text: Because the content-length header is always correct, so the loop is only a backup
options.why: The header is whatever the caller wrote, and a chunked request has none. Only counting real bytes can be trusted.

check.q: A caller sends {"text": "hi" (the closing brace is missing). Which answer is right?

options.why: An exception in our code is not always our fault. Here the caller sent broken JSON, and 500 would send us looking for a bug we do not have.

options.text: 413, because the body could not be read
options.why: 413 means too large. This body is tiny; it is just not valid JSON.

options.text: 400, because the request itself is wrong
options.why: The catch turns a SyntaxError from JSON.parse into 400: the caller can fix it by sending valid JSON.

p: The broker and the gateway are plain node:http servers, like Byte's broker that ours starts from: one handler, a route string, /health without authentication for Kubernetes, 404 for anything unknown, and a status chosen from the error type. The broker keeps Byte's 1 MiB body limit. The gateway has no limit of its own, because an agent session sends several megabytes per call and Anthropic limits the size itself.

The gateway also runs a second small server in the same process, on port 9090, for its metrics. Its access log holds the method, path, status and time of each request and never a body, and a test fails if any request text reaches the logs.

tickets.why: The broker keeps Byte's node:http core: /health without auth, 401 for the rest, and the 1 MiB body limit.
The gateway's handler: /health, two POST routes, 404 for the rest, and 401 or 502 chosen from the error type.
The broker's git proxy adds routes to the same server and streams the push through.
The metrics port is a second createServer in the same process.

words.plain: The one function createServer calls for every request, with req (what came in) and res (what you send back).
A method plus a path, such as POST /v1/comments, that your handler knows how to answer.
The number at the start of every response: 2xx worked, 4xx the caller's mistake, 5xx ours.
The most bytes a request body may have before the server stops reading and answers 413.
Node's type for raw bytes. A request body arrives as a stream of Buffer chunks.

review.q: From memory: which status does each of these get, 201, 400, 401, 404, 405, 413 or 500? A new comment, a missing token, a body over 1 MiB, a broken JSON body, an unknown path, DELETE on a path that only allows GET and POST, and a bug in our code.
review.a: 201 created, 401 missing token, 413 body too large, 400 broken JSON, 404 unknown path, 405 wrong method on a known path, 500 our bug.

review.q: A teammate proposes Express for the broker "so we get routing and body parsing without writing them". What would you say?
review.a: The broker holds the credentials, so every line in it should be readable in one review. node:http with a route string, a counted body and a status on every path is a few dozen lines, has no dependencies to audit, and matches Byte's broker that ours starts from. Express's body parser would still need its limit set by hand.

remember: One handler sees every request: match the route yourself, count the body against a limit, and end every path with a status.
